title: German Occupation Administration Takes Shape
subtitle: Occupation Administration — October 26, 1939
body:
A government for conquest

On October 26, 1939, Germany gave its occupation of Poland a new administrative structure. In the west and north, conquered territory was being incorporated into the Reich. Farther east, Hans Frank assumed civilian authority over the General Government, a separate territory administered for German purposes. For the inhabitants, the distinction would affect which officials governed them, which laws applied, and whether their homes stood in an area marked for German settlement. Neither arrangement restored Polish self-government. Both made the consequences of military defeat more enduring by placing them in the hands of administrators, police officers, economic officials, and institutions empowered to issue further orders. [1]

The [September 28 treaty](/articles/german-soviet-boundary-treaty-1939-09-28) had divided the occupiers’ spheres and asserted their authority to reorganize them. October’s decisions addressed the next question: what would German rule actually require? The answer was more complicated than replacing Polish flags and officeholders. Germany wanted productive land, factories, strategic communications, and labor, while its racial policy required the destruction of Polish political independence and the transformation of selected territories into German settlement areas. These ambitions could reinforce one another, but they also produced friction. A population that officials wanted removed might include workers an industrial enterprise needed; a territory designated to receive deportees still required food and functioning services. The emerging administration inherited these contradictions. [2] [3] Three decrees supplied the framework. Hitler’s October 7 decree on strengthening German nationhood—*Festigung deutschen Volkstums*—gave Heinrich Himmler responsibility for bringing ethnic Germans into the Reich’s orbit, establishing settlements, and eliminating the influence of populations defined as threatening to German interests. The decree combined resettlement with coercion from its inception: Himmler could take general and administrative measures to carry out that racial program. Its categories expressed Nazi ideology, not objective differences in people’s entitlement to live in their own country. [4] The decree dated October 8, *über Gliederung und Verwaltung der Ostgebiete*, concerned the organization and administration of the eastern territories to be incorporated into Germany. The decree dated October 12, *über die Verwaltung der besetzten polnischen Gebiete*, addressed the occupied Polish territories outside those annexations. Its first sections placed that remainder under a governor general, appointed Frank, and made him directly subordinate to Hitler. October 26 was the effective administrative changeover, rather than the date on which all three instruments had been issued. The annexation decree initially specified November 1; a further decree of October 20 advanced its operation to October 26. [5] [6]

Reading the documents

An official date is not the whole chronology

The General Government’s founding decree bears the date October 12, but its final clause tied implementation to Hitler’s withdrawal of the army’s administrative mandate. That occurred at the end of October 25. A decree’s date, the transfer of authority, and the completion of the offices created under it were separate events. The resulting system continued to take shape after Frank formally assumed power. [6]

Choosing the territory—and changing its population

The annexed lands did not form one uniform province. The October settlement created Reichsgaue, territorial units combining state administration with Nazi Party power, at West Prussia and Posen. The former became Danzig–West Prussia on November 2; the latter received the name Wartheland on January 29, 1940. Those familiar later names can obscure the sequence. Posen, centered on Poznań, was governed by Arthur Greiser; Albert Forster headed the northern unit, which brought together the former Free City of Danzig, much of Polish Pomerania and the Corridor, and territory previously administered within German East Prussia. [7] Danzig requires a qualification. Before the war, it was a Free City under League of Nations protection, with specified Polish rights; it was not simply another province of the Polish Republic. German incorporation of Danzig and annexation of sovereign Polish territory were therefore distinct acts, even when the occupation subsequently placed them within the same administrative unit. Elsewhere, Germany enlarged existing provinces. The Ciechanów region went into East Prussia, while Polish Upper Silesia, including Katowice, was attached to Silesia. Describing every annexed district as part of either Posen or Danzig–West Prussia would erase these important differences. [8] [1] Łódź illustrates how unsettled the boundary initially remained. The city’s incorporation followed in November, with November 9 identified in the administrative chronology, rather than being a completed fact of October 26. Nor should its later German name, Litzmannstadt, be projected backward: that renaming occurred in 1940. What would become the Wartheland consequently included substantial territory beyond Germany’s pre-1914 frontier. German annexation was not merely an attempt to reverse the Treaty of Versailles. It expanded the Reich into areas whose Polish population and institutions the occupiers then intended to subordinate or displace. [7] [9] [10] The economic attraction was substantial. These annexations took in important agricultural and industrial regions; Upper Silesia brought industrial capacity, while the western territories offered productive farmland. Göring’s instructions of October 19 made the intended distinction explicit: areas incorporated into Germany were to have their productive resources preserved and developed within the German economy. The General Government was to surrender raw materials, machinery, and enterprises useful to the German war effort. Territory, population, and economic assets were being assigned different purposes within the same project of domination. [10] [3] The racial objective explains why this was not simply an administrative division between richer and poorer regions. Himmler’s October 7 mandate treated settlement as a state undertaking and authorized the assignment of new living areas. The officials making these decisions did not regard existing residence or Polish citizenship as sufficient protection against removal. Annexation was meant to enable demographic transformation, rather than merely to acknowledge a supposedly German character already present. Ethnic Germans arriving from abroad could become beneficiaries of a program whose implementation required the dispossession of others. That connection was built into the responsibilities given to Himmler, even though the scale and procedures of later deportations were still developing. [4] This also helps explain why Germany did not annex everything it occupied. In the record of Hitler’s October 17 conference with Wilhelm Keitel, the remaining Polish territory was assigned a low standard of living, a supply of labor, and a military role. Roads, railways, and communications were to remain useful to Germany, while the emergence of an independent Polish leadership was to be prevented. The area would also receive people removed from the Reich. Keeping it outside direct incorporation allowed the regime to exploit and police its inhabitants without undertaking to absorb them into the national community it claimed to be constructing. This was a deliberate allocation of functions, although particular borders and practices remained subject to argument. [2]

Frank’s authority, and its limits

The General Government began with four districts: Kraków, Warsaw, Radom, and Lublin. Galicia was added only in 1941. Frank, a lawyer and longstanding Nazi, presided over an administration in which German district heads and subordinate officials exercised authority over occupied communities. The October 26 organizational ordinance designated Kraków as his official seat. This was a German governmental decision, not a transfer of the Polish Republic’s capital: Warsaw’s reduced place in the occupation hierarchy did not make it cease to be Poland’s capital in Polish political life. [1] [6] Kraków’s selection also belonged to the practical redrawing of the occupation’s administrative geography. Frank initially operated from Łódź, whose impending incorporation into the Reich made it unsuitable as the lasting seat of the separate General Government. The documentary history records his official move to Kraków in early November. The distinction between a designated seat and the movement of the governor’s office is useful: the establishment of civilian rule was a process conducted amid disputes over jurisdiction and territory, not a completed government appearing everywhere at midnight. [5] The founding decree conferred extensive authority on Frank, but also contained the seeds of competing claims. He answered directly to Hitler and was assigned all branches of administration. Yet the Reich Defense Council and Göring, as plenipotentiary for the Four-Year Plan, could also legislate for the territory. Reich authorities retained powers connected with wider German economic planning; the finance minister had to approve Frank’s budget, and the occupied territory itself was to bear the costs of administration. Frank’s government thus possessed a separate administrative identity without acquiring sovereign independence. Its inhabitants were expected to finance the machinery imposed on them. [6] Police authority exposed a further contradiction. Frank’s October 26 security ordinance described the Higher SS and Police Leader as responsible to him and required his consent on matters of fundamental importance. In other matters, that official could act independently and issue police regulations. Alongside this formal relationship stood the SS hierarchy under Himmler. The General Government consequently contained overlapping channels of power rather than an ordinary civil administration with a wholly subordinate police service. Frank’s signature on the ordinance also matters: conflict over jurisdiction did not make him an opponent of coercion. His own government authorized the police powers through which repression would operate. [6] [11] The army’s withdrawal from general administration did not signify the end of military interests or a transition from violence to restraint. Hitler’s October 17 conference explicitly preserved the territory’s strategic importance, including the maintenance of communications for military use. The same record instructed the administration to prevent Polish political consolidation and denied that familiar legal restrictions should impede its racial objectives. Here the contrast with Hitler’s October 6 public speech is especially revealing. Before the Reichstag he had advertised peace, restored economic life, and the possible formation of a restricted Polish state; in the internal discussion, subsistence, labor extraction, and the suppression of leadership defined the assignment. [2] [12] Proposals for a residual Polish state therefore require careful handling. Hitler mentioned one publicly, and the October 17 memorandum itself used the language of Polish “independence.” But its accompanying instructions excluded independent political organization and placed the population under German control. These words did not establish a Polish government or a negotiated settlement. The General Government was what Germany actually created: an occupation apparatus accountable upward to the German leadership. Its future was not fixed in every detail, but its inhabitants had no authorized means of deciding it. [12] [2]

Occupation at the counter, the workplace, and the school

The new order did not abolish every existing institution. Section 4 of the October 12 decree retained existing law insofar as it did not contradict Germany’s assumption of administration. That condition was decisive. Continuity served the occupier’s convenience and could be withdrawn when German policy required it. On October 26, a separate ordinance provided for both German and Polish jurisdictions, reserving to German courts the protection of German security, prestige, persons, and property. Polish courts were therefore permitted a subordinate role rather than recognized as the judicial authority of an independent state. Detailed arrangements continued to follow; the whole later court system should not be imagined as complete on its first day. [6] This selective preservation reached into municipal life. German rule still required people who could keep local records and carry out ordinary administrative work. The November 28 municipal ordinance subsequently made the hierarchy explicit: mayors were responsible for municipal administration and finances, but their appointment and supervision belonged to the occupation authorities. Keeping a Polish official at a desk did not preserve the public authority that desk had represented before the invasion. Nor does continued service by itself explain an individual’s conduct. Maintaining necessary services, protecting neighbors, obeying coercive orders, and assisting persecution were different actions, whose circumstances and consequences have to be examined rather than collapsed into a single label. [6] One of Frank’s first measures reached directly into personal identity. The October 26 *Kennkarte* ordinance required identity cards for the Polish population of the General Government. They were to record name, birth and descent, marital status, occupation, religion, and state affiliation, and to include a fingerprint. Implementation was entrusted to the Higher SS and Police Leader. The order did not mean that every inhabitant received a new document that day. It did establish the administrative ambition: individuals would become legible to the occupation through a set of officially recorded characteristics, including characteristics the regime used to distribute privileges and impose persecution. [6] Labor regulations made unequal treatment explicit. The October 26 ordinance imposed a public labor obligation on Polish inhabitants aged eighteen to sixty, while providing separate rules for Jews. It specified agricultural work, public construction, transport infrastructure, and land improvement; people able to demonstrate continuing socially useful employment were not supposed to be called up under this particular obligation. Such qualifications did not make the system voluntary. They show how an administration could claim the power to allocate labor while distinguishing between those it considered already usefully employed and those it intended to direct elsewhere. [6] The parallel decree for Jews introduced compulsory labor and envisaged forced-labor groups, with implementation assigned to the SS and police leader. These were two differently organized mechanisms, issued on the same date. Polish Jews were citizens of the same republic, but Nazi administration separated them through racial categories and subjected them to additional persecution. Later measures widened the machinery: in December, district authorities received permission to extend the general Polish labor obligation to fourteen-to-eighteen-year-olds. That later extension should not be substituted for the original October age range. [6] Education reveals the same combination of practical dependence and political destruction. On October 31, Frank ordered the reopening of Polish elementary and vocational schools while separating German and Polish pupils and teachers. Polish private schools required permission; the ordinance reserved higher educational institutions for further regulation. The policy allowed forms of schooling useful to a subordinated workforce while denying any general guarantee of autonomous intellectual life. It was followed on November 6 by the arrest of Kraków academics summoned to hear a German official’s address. That attack belongs to the weeks after the administrative changeover, but it demonstrates how little protection the appearance of civilian government offered to established Polish institutions. [6] [13] Cultural control also had an immediate bureaucratic form. An October 26 ordinance made the publication, printing, and distribution of printed material dependent on permission. It covered both periodical and nonperiodical publications, placing more than the daily press at the administration’s disposal. For a teacher, publisher, religious association, or political group, the ability to communicate could now depend on authorization from an occupying power committed to preventing Polish political organization. The destruction of national life involved these routine controls as well as spectacular acts of violence: an office able to refuse permission could silence activity without having to close every institution by force on the same day. [6] [2]

Property, displacement, and terror

Göring’s October 19 economic instructions illuminate what administrative “order” meant for property. He demanded centralized custody of assets taken from Polish hands through the Main Trustee Office East, the *Haupttreuhandstelle Ost*, and described arrangements for state property and private Polish and Jewish property. The office could appoint administrators and replace ones installed by other agencies. Local confiscations were subject to confirmation. Göring condemned unauthorized seizures and private enrichment, but the purpose was to secure the proceeds for the Reich. Regulating confiscation did not restore the owners’ rights; it established which German institution should control what had been taken. [3] The same instructions also acknowledged an awkward economic fact: the newly divided regions had belonged to a connected economy. Göring claimed central direction from Berlin despite their different political treatment. His order to remove useful machinery from the General Government contained a revealing exception—where transfer would take too long, enterprises could fulfill German orders where they stood. This was exploitation adjusted to practical constraints. It helps explain why deprivation and the preservation of selected productive activity could coexist. A factory might remain open because its output was valuable to Germany, without that decision implying concern for the rights or prosperity of its Polish owners and workers. [3] Displacement was already more than a future program. In Gdynia, expulsions began in October, before the formal establishment of the General Government. Polish residents lost access to homes in a port the Germans intended to use for their own purposes. At the same time, ethnic Germans were arriving from the Baltic region: Monika Tomkiewicz’s account records arrivals at Gdańsk on October 15 and at Gdynia on October 24. Not every arrival remained in the port, and the later settlement apparatus should not be read back into each early movement. Even so, removal and reception were already operating together, turning racial plans into demands for housing, transport, property, and administrative decisions. [14] [15] The population categories concealed considerable human variety. People classified as ethnic Germans did not all possess the same background, political conduct, or relationship to Germany. Ethnic Poles and Polish Jews likewise differed in class, religion, political commitments, and local experience, while the General Government also contained Ukrainian communities and other minorities. These differences did not prevent German authorities from assigning collective positions within an unequal order. Himmler’s mandate treated supposedly dangerous populations as objects of policy; Frank’s labor decrees separated Jews from other Polish inhabitants. Such categories were instruments imposed on society, not adequate descriptions of everyone placed within them. [4] [6] [16] [5] Terror had preceded the new administrative framework and continued through it. Einsatzgruppen, SS and police units, German military personnel, and the ethnic German *Selbstschutz* participated in attacks on civilians. Officials, clergy, teachers, landowners, and other potential sources of organized Polish leadership were among those targeted. The US Holocaust Memorial Museum’s photographic collection documents executions around Bydgoszcz and Toruń in autumn 1939, including teachers killed near Fordon and civilians guarded by SS and Selbstschutz members near Tuchola. These records locate the violence in particular places and organizations. They do not permit the comforting separation of administrative history from the murder of the people an administration intended to dominate. [17] The autumn campaign against Polish elites, commonly associated with the *Intelligenzaktion*, must be distinguished from the AB-Aktion of spring 1940. Auschwitz was also a later development, not a camp already operating at this October changeover. For Jews, humiliation, forced labor, dispossession, and expulsion were already realities, but the later extermination system cannot be projected backward as an institution fully formed in 1939. The General Government’s general armband decree was issued on November 23 and took effect on December 1, although local badge requirements had appeared earlier. These distinctions do not diminish the crimes already committed. They make it possible to identify the decisions through which persecution expanded. [18] [15] [19] [6]

A resident’s recollection

Covering the windows in Gdynia

Jadwiga Kocuniak later recalled sheltering with her family in a friend’s building on Świętojańska Street when German troops entered Gdynia. Soldiers shouted orders to cover the windows and not look out, threatening to shoot. Preserved in Monika Tomkiewicz’s account, the recollection concerns the occupation’s first days, before October’s administrative settlement. It conveys the immediate coercion behind the official language of restored order. [15]

Polish continuity under occupation

For Polish society, the administrative division multiplied the pressures created by defeat. A family’s home, workplace, and relatives could fall under different authorities; refugees attempting to return confronted guarded crossings, missing documents, and the risk of arrest. The museum’s research on refugees records that some returned toward German-occupied territory despite its dangers, driven by exhaustion and the hope of reaching home. Such choices should not be mistaken for acceptance of the new order. They show how decisions about safety were made with limited resources and incomplete information, while occupation authorities controlled routes and permissions. [20] Political continuity developed on a different plane. Władysław Raczkiewicz succeeded to the presidency, and General Władysław Sikorski headed the Polish government established in France. Their authority did not depend on recognition by the occupiers. In a September 30 communication to Washington, Ambassador Jerzy Potocki explicitly rejected the German–Soviet partition agreement as illegal and reaffirmed Poland’s intention to restore its territory and its people’s rights. The [previous chapter](/articles/german-soviet-boundary-treaty-1939-09-28#poland-refuses) examines that protest in its diplomatic setting. By October 26, its relevance had become even more concrete: Germany was creating administrations over a country whose government continued to reject the premise on which they rested. [21] [22] Inside occupied Poland, organized resistance was also beginning to take institutional form. On September 27, General Michał Tokarzewski-Karaszewicz began building *Służba Zwycięstwu Polski*, the Service for Poland’s Victory. The organization represented an early attempt to sustain coordinated struggle after the collapse of open military defense. It was not yet the Home Army. Sikorski created the Union of Armed Struggle in November 1939; the Home Army name followed in 1942. Keeping these stages separate preserves something important about October: clandestine structures had to be built under conditions of uncertainty, surveillance, and repression, rather than simply continuing as an already complete underground state. [21] The coexistence of legal survival abroad and precarious organization at home defined Poland’s position. Diplomatic representatives could reject annexation and retain recognition; people under occupation still had to find food, maintain households, and navigate institutions controlled by Germany. Neither kind of action made the other unnecessary. Refusing the partition preserved a political claim that the occupiers wanted extinguished, while preserving social relationships and the capacity to organize kept that claim connected to a population. This was not a uniform national experience: the additional racial persecution directed against Jews profoundly altered the dangers they faced. The evidence supports a history of related but unequal experiences, rather than a single imagined response shared by every Polish citizen. [22] [21] [6]

Moscow’s parallel settlement, and the Western refusal

East of the partition line, the Soviet authorities were constructing a different justification for territorial absorption. Controlled elections on October 22 produced assemblies presented as expressions of popular will. The People’s Assembly of Western Ukraine met in Lviv from October 26 to 28; the Western Belorussian assembly met in Białystok later that month. German civilian administration and Soviet annexation therefore did not begin as identical legal acts on October 26. Soviet incorporation proceeded through further decisions in November, with the USSR’s Supreme Soviet acting on Western Ukraine on November 1 and Western Belarus on November 2. [23] [24] The Western Ukrainian assembly’s October 27 declaration proclaimed Soviet power and asserted unanimous popular consent. Read alongside the controlled electoral process, it records what the occupation wanted to claim, rather than demonstrating freely expressed agreement. Soviet consolidation also involved the NKVD and the persecution of people classified as enemies of the new order. Polish citizens of Jewish background could escape immediate exposure to Nazi racial persecution yet face Soviet attacks on private enterprise, religious and political institutions, or alleged “counterrevolutionary” activity. Their varied circumstances rule out treating either relief at German withdrawal or support from some individuals as consent on behalf of entire communities. [25] [26] Berlin and Moscow could cooperate without organizing their territories in the same way. An American diplomatic report of October 9 recorded the arrival in Moscow of German economic negotiators, including representatives concerned with agriculture and railways, together with the head of the German frontier commission. This was the practical continuation of the settlement described in the earlier treaty chapter: frontiers, population arrangements, and economic cooperation all required implementation. The two governments shared an interest in consolidating their territorial gains and obstructing the return of independent Polish power. Their differing racial, social, and political programs nevertheless remained essential to understanding how each exercised control. [27] [22] Britain’s response challenged the political finality Germany sought. In the House of Commons on October 12, Neville Chamberlain argued that Hitler’s proposals required acceptance of his conquests and his claimed freedom to deal with conquered peoples. Britain would not accept that foundation for peace. Chamberlain also cited Édouard Daladier’s October 10 broadcast, emphasizing French agreement that fighting could not end without dependable security. France’s hosting of the Polish government gave that refusal a concrete institutional expression. Recognition, however, did not give either Western ally the immediate ability to dismantle the administrations being established inside Poland. Diplomatic continuity and the occupiers’ physical control existed simultaneously. [28] [21] The United States supplied a particularly clear statement of the distinction while remaining outside the war. On October 2, Secretary of State Cordell Hull affirmed that seizure of territory did not extinguish a government’s legal existence and that American recognition of Poland continued. The statement is reproduced in a later American briefing paper, which should not be confused with a fresh declaration issued in 1945. Hull’s position did not prevent German officials from administering annexed districts or Frank from issuing decrees. It denied that those acts alone settled the international question of Poland’s existence. Germany had achieved control over territory without securing general acceptance of the political conclusion it drew from that control. [10]

Control without consent

October 26 established a framework capable of producing further coercion. Annexation authorities could pursue German settlement and incorporation; the General Government could regulate labor, classify inhabitants, supervise surviving Polish institutions, and direct resources toward German needs. Authority was divided and sometimes contested, yet those conflicts did not protect the governed. A civilian administrator, a police official, and an economic agency could disagree over jurisdiction while contributing to the same process of dispossession. The decrees are revealing because they connect ambitious political objectives to ordinary administrative acts: appointing an official, recording an identity, assigning work, approving a publication, or taking control of an enterprise. [6] [3] What these arrangements could not provide was Polish consent or an internationally accepted extinction of the Polish Republic. The government in France, the beginnings of organized resistance at home, and continued foreign recognition contradicted Germany’s claim that conquest had closed the matter. Soviet incorporation was advancing through its own coercive procedures, rather than resolving that contradiction. Poland’s inhabitants now faced governments with immense power over their daily lives; Poland’s political existence nevertheless survived the loss of control over its territory. The occupation settlement made domination more systematic. It did not turn the occupiers’ power to issue orders into the authority of a settlement accepted by the people and state they had conquered. [22] [10] [21]
author: R.G. Cruise
location: German-occupied Poland, with responses from Moscow and the Western capitals
summary: Annexation and the General Government gave conquest different administrative forms. The decrees, property offices, labor orders, and police powers reveal how German rule took shape—and why control of Poland did not extinguish the Polish state.

sourceMethod: The chapter uses contemporary decrees, diplomatic correspondence, the October 17 Hitler–Keitel conference record, and parliamentary proceedings alongside museum research and scholarly documentary history. Nazi and Soviet declarations are read as evidence of policy and official claims, not as proof of consent or legitimacy. The General Government documents were checked in the German transcriptions reproduced in Documenta Occupationis VI; the relevant printed pages are identified below. Selected sections of scholarly works were consulted, not the complete volumes. Daladier’s October 10 broadcast is accessed through Chamberlain’s October 12 parliamentary statement; Hull’s October 2 declaration through its reproduction in a 1945 American briefing paper. Measures in force on October 26 are distinguished from later implementation and subsequent decrees.
